title: Regex — where it stands
eyebrow: Capability positioning · read from the source, not from memory
thesis: Under the hood it is PCRE2 10.47, statically linked, Unicode always on. On top sits an unusually rich Ring layer — 100+ methods, four fluent builder classes, and a reactive match→code engine — with a clear `Match()`-anchors / `MatchFirst()`-searches / partial-as-you-type model. On features it is at PCRE2 parity — lookaround, backreferences, recursion, conditionals, things RE2 and Rust deliberately refuse. Where it trails the modern engines is the safety-and-throughput story: no JIT, no linear-time matcher, and the ReDoS knob isn't even reachable from Ring — although the code for both is already compiled into the binary.
grid_title: Twelve lanes, each against its category leader
grid_lede: Every lane names what actually ships, the tools it is fair to measure against, and the one thing still owed. The recurring theme: a broad, well-guarded feature surface over a compact 17-function C engine — with the performance and safety knobs left un-wired.

lanes.engine: A well-articulated model: `Match()` anchors the whole content, `MatchFirst()` searches unanchored, `MatchAt(s,n)` from a position, and a partial "as-you-type" mode (`PARTIAL_HARD/SOFT`) for live validation. Scope helpers match within lines / words / segments.
lanes.owed: The clearest match-semantics API of the group, and the partial-match mode is a genuine plus most libraries lack. Nothing structural owed.

lanes.engine: Numbered and named captures (`(?<name>)` and `(?P<name>)`), with positions and `[start,end]` section variants. Ring re-derives names in source order because PCRE2 enumerates them alphabetically — a thoughtful correction.
lanes.owed: Comprehensive. The only related gap is on the replace side (named-group substitution, lane 5), not on capture itself.

lanes.engine: PCRE2 compiled with `UTF | UCP` unconditionally: `\p{L}`, `\p{Lu}`, scripts (`\p{Greek}`, `\p{Arabic}`), and codepoint-correct `\w`/`\d`/`.` over multibyte UTF-8, with codepoint↔byte offset conversion at the boundary.
lanes.owed: At parity — Unicode is on by default and cannot be accidentally disabled (the `:UseUnicode` flag is a no-op because it is already always on).

lanes.engine: The full PCRE2 set, all proven by engine tests: lookahead / lookbehind, backreferences `\1`, atomic `(?>)`, possessive `++`, non-capturing, recursion `(?R)`, and conditionals `(?(?=c)t|e)`.
lanes.owed: A category advantage: RE2 and Rust deliberately omit backrefs, lookaround and recursion for their linear-time guarantee. Softanza has them — at the cost of that guarantee (lane 11).

lanes.engine: Engine-backed replace with backreferences `$1` / `${1}` / `\1` and literal `$$`, via global `StzRegexReplace` and the string face `ReplaceRegex`.
lanes.owed: Named-group substitution (`${name}`) is parsed but only numeric names are honored; and there is no `Replace` method on the `stzRegex` object itself — only the global and string-face routes.

lanes.engine: Find-all comes two ways: the string face's single-pass `FindAllRegex` / `extract_all` (O(n), skips UTF-8 re-validation), and the `stzRegex` iteration wrappers (`Matches`, `MatchesZZ`). Split via `SplitByRegex`.
lanes.owed: The `stzRegex` iteration path makes a per-match engine round-trip (slower than the string-face single pass), and `split_get` silently caps at 512 pieces (fixed stack arrays).

lanes.engine: The standard modifiers — case-insensitive, dot-all, multiline, extended, non-greedy — plus auto-multiline when the pattern contains a newline. A pattern compiles once and recompiles only when flags change; anchor/partial changes are free (match-time options).
lanes.owed: Several advertised flags are no-ops (`:DontCapture`, `:DisableOptimizations`, `:UseUnicode`), and there is no cross-object compiled-pattern cache.

lanes.engine: A distinctive surface most regex libraries lack: four builders — `stzRegexMaker` (declarative classes, groups, quantifiers), `stzRecursiveRegexMaker`, `stzConditionalRegexMaker` (the `W` conditional DSL → `(?(?=c)t|e)`), and `stzRegexLookaroundMaker` — each emitting a pattern string.
lanes.owed: Unfinished in spots: `Quantifiers()` is an empty `#TODO`, `MatchSameContentAs` has a parameter-name bug, and `NumberOfSequences()` reads an undefined global — latent errors if called.

lanes.engine: `stzRegexuter` — a trigger→pattern→code engine that runs regex over text and evaluates per-match code referencing `@value`, with state tracking, dependency chains and per-position results. Ties into Softanza's broader `When/If/Do` convention.
lanes.owed: A novel niche surface — powerful, but built on `eval()` and narrower in use than the core matcher. Rated as the distinctive extra it is.

lanes.engine: A 4,842-line catalogue (`stzRegexData.ring`) of named patterns with explanations, reached by `rxp()` / `pat()` — a real asset for "email/url/date" without hand-writing the pattern.
lanes.owed: `Explain()` works only for named patterns — the fallback calls `new stzRegexAnalyzer(...)`, a class that does not exist in the library, so explaining an arbitrary pattern raises rather than explains.

lanes.engine: One matching path: PCRE2's standard backtracking `pcre2_match`. Correct, Unicode-aware, and fast on typical patterns.
lanes.owed: Both faster paths are compiled into the binary but never called: `pcre2_jit_compile` (JIT off) and `pcre2_dfa_match` (the linear, no-backtracking matcher). The code that would answer RE2's whole advantage is present and dark.

lanes.engine: The engine has the guards: `stz_regex_set_limits(steps, input_len, depth)` bounds a catastrophic pattern (an engine test proves `(a+)+$` aborts), with a ~10M-step default and a 64 MB input cap.
lanes.owed: The limits API is bridged but not surfaced on the Ring `stzRegex` class — no method calls it — so a caller cannot actually tune the bound against a hostile pattern. Backtracking means ReDoS is bounded, never eliminated.

gaps_title: The gaps, ordered by return — not by size
gaps_lede: Three tiers. The first is where the highest leverage sits — because the code is already in the binary; the second is cheap correctness; the third is throughput and reach.

tiers.title: Tier A — foundational (and the code already ships)

items.title: Wire the linear-time DFA matcher
items.text: `pcre2_dfa_match` is compiled into the binary and never called. Exposing it as an opt-in matcher gives a no-backtracking, ReDoS-immune path for the patterns that don't need backrefs — answering RE2/Rust's core advantage with code that is already present.

items.title: Surface the ReDoS limits on the Ring class
items.text: `stz_regex_set_limits` is bridged but unreachable from `stzRegex`. A method that sets step/depth/input bounds turns an existing safety mechanism into one a caller can actually use against a hostile pattern.

items.title: Named-group substitution in replace
items.text: Honor `${name}` in replacement strings (it is already parsed, just not expanded for non-numeric names). A small fix that closes an obvious surprise.

items.title: Fix the broken explain & builder stubs
items.text: Provide the missing `stzRegexAnalyzer` (or drop the fallback), and close the RegexMaker latent bugs — `Quantifiers()` TODO, `MatchSameContentAs` param name, `NumberOfSequences` undefined global.

items.title: Raise the split cap
items.text: `split_get` truncates at 512 pieces through fixed stack arrays — the same class of bug the byte and string engines carry. Grow the buffer or return count-then-drain.

items.title: Enable PCRE2 JIT
items.text: `pcre2_jit_compile` is in the build source list but never invoked. Wiring it (with the interpreter as fallback) is the standard throughput win for hot patterns.

items.title: Regex over lists, not just strings
items.text: The `stzRegex` TODO names it: apply a pattern across a list of items in one call. A natural fit with the collections plane and a real ergonomics win.

items.title: A cross-object pattern cache
items.text: Today each `stzRegex` compiles its own pattern; a shared LRU cache keyed on pattern+flags would spare repeated compiles across a program, matching Python's implicit cache.

notes.lead: The honesty line on the ratings.
notes.text: The two test runners disagree: `_ERR_RUN.txt` (current filenames) shows all 53 regex and 51 maker files run crash-free, but the assertion-marker runner `_RUN.txt` is stale — its filenames predate the current layout — and reports failures clustered in recursive-match info shape and `CaptureXT`. So the "does not crash" guarantee is firm; the assertion-level one is partly unverifiable until that runner is refreshed. The Zig in-source tests (~57 blocks) are the most trustworthy proof, including three that guard a real subject-lifetime heap bug.

Softanza's regex is a feature-complete PCRE2 with the friendliest match-semantics API and builder surface in its class — and a performance story that is one wiring job away from RE2's league, because the linear-time matcher, the JIT and the ReDoS limits are all already in the binary, just not called.

Ratings reflect what the guards prove.
